primary_claim: Deception probes (logistic classifiers on internal activations), used via simple full-token-averaging, catch 97% of deceptive responses at a 1% false-positive rate on honest responses and outperform black-box monitoring on most of five strategic-deception datasets, replicating and extending Apollo Research's earlier findings.

effect.metric: TPR at 1% FPR (deception probe, Full Averaging, control = Alpaca)
effect.value: 97% TPR at 1% FPR, i.e. catching 97% of deceptive responses while misclassifying only 1% of honest responses

contradicts_or_qualifies: Replicates and extends Apollo Research's deception probe findings (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes'), which showed >96% TPR at 1% FPR

Departs from Redwood's typical control-evaluation setup where the untrusted model is stronger than the trusted monitor; here the trusted monitor (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) is stronger than the untrusted model (Llama 3.3 70B)
stated_future_work: Thinking about novel applications for deception probes: trusted monitoring, scalable alignment, eliciting latent knowledge, detecting sandbagging and alignment-faking
Stress-testing deception probe training and deployment against adversarial strategies
Further work should validate the results on model organisms where hidden information is induced by finetuning rather than prompting
limitations_stated: Probes are noisy; sophisticated aggregation methods (peak, critical-token averaging, follow-up question probing) performed worse than simply averaging all probe scores
'Deception dilution' (padding deceptive responses with irrelevant truths) had a smaller effect than expected, but Full Averaging remains vulnerable to it in principle

Obscuring the system prompt/scratchpad from monitors as a proxy for the model's internal information may be methodologically dubious, since private tokens could influence the residual stream of public tokens differently than true internal reasoning would
quote: we replicate and extend Apollo's findings, catching 97% of the deceptive responses while misclassifying only 1% of honest responses
